content.user_title: Build Attack Trees for Security Planning
content.value_statement: Security teams need a clear way to compare attack paths and defense gaps. This skill structures attack trees, scoring, diagrams, and mitigation priorities.
actual_capabilities: Defines attack tree node types, attributes, and mitigation fields.
Provides Python templates for building and scoring attack trees.
Exports modeled trees to Mermaid and PlantUML diagram formats.
Analyzes easiest, cheapest, stealthiest, and open attack paths.
Prioritizes mitigations by path coverage and critical node impact.
limitations: It does not execute attacks or validate vulnerabilities in live systems.
It depends on accurate threat inputs from the user or security team.
Generated scores are qualitative planning aids, not measured exploit probabilities.
Examples may need adaptation for each organization, asset, and control environment.

use_cases.title: Review Application Threat Paths
use_cases.description: Map ways an attacker could reach a sensitive asset and compare control gaps before design approval.

use_cases.title: Prioritize Mitigation Work
use_cases.description: Rank mitigations by the number of attack paths they reduce, then plan security backlog items.

use_cases.title: Plan Authorized Exercises
use_cases.description: Structure permitted attack scenarios into clear goals, subgoals, attributes, and expected detections.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Tree
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a simple attack tree for [system]. Include root goal, major subgoals, leaf attacks, and likely mitigations.

prompt_templates.title: Score Attack Paths
prompt_templates.prompt: Using this threat context: [details], assign difficulty, cost, time, and detection risk to each leaf attack.

prompt_templates.title: Generate Diagrams
prompt_templates.prompt: Convert this attack tree into Mermaid and PlantUML formats. Keep labels concise and mark OR, AND, and leaf nodes.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze Mitigation Coverage
prompt_templates.prompt: Analyze this attack tree and control list: [tree and controls]. Identify open paths, critical nodes, and prioritized mitigations.

output_examples.input: Account takeover risk for a consumer web app.
output: Root goal: take over a user account.
Major branches: steal credentials, bypass authentication, and manipulate account recovery.
Priority mitigations: MFA, rate limiting, breached password checks, and support verification.

output_examples.input: Threat model review for a cloud admin console.
output: The tree separates identity abuse, session compromise, and privileged action misuse.
Open paths depend on weak admin MFA, broad service roles, and limited alert coverage.
Recommended focus: privileged access review, session controls, and high-risk action alerts.

output_examples.input: Mitigation planning after an authorized red team exercise.
output: Critical nodes appear in multiple successful paths and should receive owners first.
Coverage improves most by addressing credential reuse, recovery workflow checks, and endpoint alerts.

best_practices: Start with a specific attacker goal and asset boundary.
Capture assumptions for difficulty, cost, time, and detection ratings.
Review trees with defenders, engineers, and authorized testing teams.
anti_patterns: Using attack trees as step-by-step offensive instructions.
Assigning scores without evidence or stakeholder review.
Leaving leaf attacks without mapped mitigations or owners.

faq.question: What is an attack tree?
faq.answer: It is a structured model that breaks an attacker goal into possible paths, dependencies, and leaf attack steps.

faq.question: Does this skill run security tools?
faq.answer: No. It provides modeling templates and analysis guidance, not scanning or exploitation.

faq.question: Can it create diagrams?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes guidance for Mermaid and PlantUML exports from a modeled tree.

faq.question: Who should use this skill?
faq.answer: Security architects, product security teams, red teams, and risk owners can use it for authorized assessments.

faq.question: How should I score difficulty?
faq.answer: Use known controls, required access, attacker skill, time, cost, and detection likelihood.

faq.question: Is this appropriate for offensive use?
faq.answer: Use it only for authorized threat modeling, security planning, or approved assessments.
